content.text:
## TOPIC 1 — Nadia Eghbal / Nadia Asparouhova

**Note on citations:** no reliable page numbers exist online for *Working in Public*. The most trustworthy verbatim source I found is Mark Nagelberg's Kindle-highlight notes (https://www.marknagelberg.com/roam-notes-on-working-in-public-by-nadia-eghbal/), which carry **Kindle location numbers** — I use those. Goodreads' quotes page is a second verified source. I flag paraphrases separately; several "quote" aggregator sites (sobrief, superbook, antoinebuteau.com) appear to contain LLM-generated pseudo-quotes and I have **excluded** anything I could not corroborate.

### A. The core argument (the thesis in her own words)

The single most load-bearing quote — this is the book's thesis, from the Introduction:

> **"The problem facing maintainers today is not how to get more contributors but how to manage a high volume of frequent, low-touch interactions. These developers aren't building communities; they're directing air traffic."** — Location 134

Paired with, immediately before it (Location 129):

> **"The role of a maintainer is evolving. Rather than coordinating with a group of developers, these maintainers are defined by the need for curation: sifting through the noise of interactions, such as user questions, bug reports, and feature requests, which compete for their attention."**

The same "air traffic controller" framing appears in her own earlier essay, so it's not a one-off:

> **"Instead of a community of active contributors, open source often looks more like a few developers playing air traffic controller to thousands of users."**
> **"The salient issue for maintainers today is less about growing contributor numbers and more about navigating the flow of developers who are clamoring for their time."**
> — "The rise of few-maintainer projects," *Increment*, May 2019, https://increment.com/open-source/the-rise-of-few-maintainer-projects/

### B. Attention is the scarce, rivalrous resource — not code, not contributions

> **"Open source code is public, but it doesn't have to be participatory: maintainers can buckle under excess demand for their attention."** — Goodreads verified, https://www.goodreads.com/work/quotes/84493736-working-in-public-the-making-and-maintenance-of-open-source-software

The economic core (Chapter 5, "Production as a One-Way Mirror"): consumption of open source is a **public good**; *production* is a **commons** where **maintainer attention is the rivalrous resource** (Location 2572).

> **"When developers make contributions, they appropriate this attention from the commons."** — Location 2584

> **"To reduce the over-appropriation of attention in open source software, we can think of its production as a one-way mirror, where we design for the parasocial, or one-sided, relationships that are endemic to stadiums, rather than for the interpersonal relationships that are associated with clubs."** — Location 2589

Her term for the mechanism: **"extractive contributions"** — contributions "where the marginal cost of reviewing and merging outweighs the marginal benefit to the project's producers (e.g. comments, questions, feature requests)" (Location 2632). She notes that **fear of appearing unsympathetic or unwelcoming is what keeps maintainers reviewing extractive contributions** (Location 2681).

The inversion of the usual moral frame:

> **"If anything, it's casual contributors who should be paying for access to maintainers, not the other way around."** — Location 3266

### C. "Not a contributor problem" — why more contributors makes it worse

The closest thing to the line you're after, from the book's framing (quoted in Julian Elve's notes, https://www.synesthesia.co.uk/2020/08/14/notes-on-eghbal-working-in-public/):

> **"I started to see the problem is not that there's a dearth of people who want to contribute to an open source project, but rather that there are too many contributors—or they're the wrong kind of contributors."**

Supporting data she uses in the Introduction:

> **"One study found that, in a sample of 275 popular GitHub projects across various programming languages, nearly half of all contributors only contributed once. These contributors accounted for less than 2% of total commits, or overall contributions."** — Location 85

> **"One study found that in more than 85% of the open source projects the researchers examined on GitHub, less than 5% of developers were responsible for over 95% of code and social interactions."** — Goodreads verified

> **"Even Wikipedia, the world's biggest online encyclopedia, and a canonical example of large-scale collaboration, has Steven Pruitt, a volunteer who's edited one-third of all the English language articles on the site."** — Goodreads verified

The tourist analogy — her argument that casual contributors are *not* community members and shouldn't be treated as such:

> **"Casual contributors are like tourists visiting New York City for a weekend. Just as we wouldn't expect, or even want, tourists to participate in local governance decisions, we shouldn't assume that casual contributors are part of a project's contributor community simply because they are physically present."** — Location 1569

And the emotional cost of the untenable version:

> **"In the absence of additional reputational or financial benefits, maintaining code for general public use quickly becomes an unpaid job you can't quit."** — Goodreads verified

A maintainer quote she uses (Goodreads verified) that captures the load shift precisely:

> **"The bigger your project becomes, the harder it is to keep the innovation you had in the beginning of your project. Suddenly you have to consider hundreds of different use-cases … Once you pass a few thousand active users, you'll notice that helping your users takes more time than actually working on your project."**

### D. The taxonomy: Federations / Clubs / Toys / Stadiums

Classified by the **ratio of contributor growth to user growth** (Location 862). Four inputs determine that ratio (Location 809): technical scope, support required, ease of participation, user adoption.

| Type | Contributors | Users | Examples (hers) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Federations** | high | high | Rust, Node.js, Linux |
| **Clubs** | high | low | niche/hobby projects |
| **Toys** | low | low | weekend/side projects |
| **Stadiums** | low | high | Babel, webpack, Bootstrap |

Her own definitions, verbatim, via the community reference site built on the book, https://project-types.github.io/:

- **Clubs:** *"Clubs are similar to meetup or hobby groups: they attract a narrow group of users, who then also become contributors because they have higher context for the project's activity and feel a sense of affinity to the group."*
- **Federations:** *"Federations are more complex to manage from a governance standpoint, so they tend to develop processes—voting, leadership positions, foundations, working groups, and technical councils."*
- **Stadiums:** high user growth, low contributor growth; a fast-growing userbase depends on one or a few maintainers; social structure is **centralized, one-to-many**, which makes **maintainer attention the primary bottleneck**.

The key structural claim about stadium load (Location 1142): projects **with** a commons (federations, clubs) are focused on solving **coordination** problems; projects **without** a commons (stadiums) are focused on **curation**, because of the scarcity of the creator's attention. This is the exact hinge of your argument: for stadiums, coordination tooling doesn't help — only curation and gatekeeping do.

Also (Location 1366):

> **"although maintainers are few in number, their impact on an open source project is far-reaching, because they're the bottleneck to everyone else's contributions."**

### E. Non-code work becomes the job (the "Growth stage")

Her four-stage project lifecycle (Location 757): Creation → Evangelism → **Growth** → (fork: pull back to closed development, or distribute the work). At the Growth stage, **"maintainers start doing more non-code than code work (e.g. triaging issues, reviewing pull requests)"** (Location 754).

She then catalogues the four attention-management strategies maintainers actually use (Location 2700):
1. **Reduce up-front costs** — CI, automated tests, bots, linters, issue/PR templates. ("Among the top hundred projects on GitHub by issue volume in 2018, 93% of projects used issue templates," Location 2806.)
2. **Make themselves less available** — including Philip Guo's **"n=1 approach"**: stay at one developer, don't accept PRs, read them as *suggestions* rather than merging them, avoiding "the technical and social costs of merging others' code" (Location 2845). Mike McQuaid (Homebrew) uses a **tiered** approach: more personal attention as someone contributes more (Location 2846).
3. **Distribute costs onto users** — user-to-user support systems (Location 2860).
4. **Increase total attention available** — recruit real co-maintainers, or fund attention (Location 2911).

On co-maintainers, note her explicit split (Location 1421): a healthy project needs **creators *and* curators**, and "developers tend to be more excited about creating, so curators are particularly valuable."

Maintenance also doesn't build the skills people are usually rewarded for (Location 1445): "Long-term maintenance does not typically sharpen your developer skills," after which maintainers either learn to enjoy project-management/leadership work, distribute the work, or **step down/disappear**.

Concrete evidence of review load, in her reporting (Location 2092):

> **"One maintainer of a large open source project told me that running his CI service took an hour and a half per pull request, yet he was expected to review and merge forty to fifty pull requests per day."**

Cost framing (Location 1931): software has **marginal maintenance costs** (a function of users — infra, dev tools, **user support**, **community moderation**) and **temporal maintenance costs** (entropy: tech debt, test infra, dependency management). She cites a 2018 Stripe study: **"developers spend 42% of their time maintaining code"** (Location 2074).

### F. On commit counts and GitHub contribution metrics mispresenting maintainer work

This is the weakest-covered area publicly, but there are two solid hooks.

**In the book** (Chapter 3, "Assessing the health of a project," Location 1673ff): she lists three success metrics — *popular*, *depended upon*, *active* — and then explicitly warns (Location 1709): **contributor count is misleading, especially for stadiums, "since this metric assumes contributors are fungible (i.e. interchangeable)."** She also notes (Location 1740) that for low-maintenance projects you have to look at activity *off* GitHub entirely (e.g. Stack Overflow) — i.e. GitHub-visible activity systematically undercounts the work.

**In her essay** "Methodologies for measuring project health" (July 2018, https://nadia.xyz/project-health): she argues the **"total number of contributors does not correlate to whether a project survives,"** because contributors are not interchangeable — casual one-off fixers differ fundamentally from maintainers who keep the project alive, and newer contributors produce lower-quality contributions. She notes many critical libraries have "just a handful of total contributors" and "only one or two active maintainers," making contributor-count metrics useless for exactly the projects that matter most. (Caveat for your argument: in this 2018 piece she *does* propose "work done" — merged PRs/commits — as a more size-agnostic health metric. Her position hardens against activity metrics by 2020.)

Related earlier essay, if you want the "stars/downloads are vanity" angle: "What success really looks like in open source" (Feb 2016), https://medium.com/@nayafia/what-success-really-looks-like-in-open-source-2dd1facaf91c (Medium 403s to automated fetch; readable in a browser).

Also useful: her curated collection **awesome-maintainers** — "Talks, blog posts, and interviews about the experience of being an open source maintainer" — https://github.com/nayafia/awesome-maintainers/

### G. Roads and Bridges (Ford Foundation, 2016)

**PDF:** https://www.fordfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/roads-and-bridges-the-unseen-labor-behind-our-digital-infrastructure.pdf
**Landing page:** https://www.fordfoundation.org/learning/library/research-reports/roads-and-bridges-the-unseen-labor-behind-our-digital-infrastructure/

I extracted the PDF text directly. Core thesis, verbatim from the Executive Summary (pp. 8–10):

> **"Our modern society—everything from hospitals to stock markets to newspapers to social media—runs on software. But take a closer look, and you'll find that the tools we use to build software are buckling under demand."**

> **"Much like roads or bridges, which anyone can walk or drive on, open source code can be used by anyone—from companies to individuals—to build software. This type of code makes up the digital infrastructure of our society today."**

> **"Just like physical infrastructure, digital infrastructure needs regular upkeep and maintenance. In the United States, over half of government spending on transportation and water infrastructure goes just to maintenance. But financial support for digital infrastructure is much harder to come by."**

The invisibility argument — the strongest line for your purposes:

> **"This increased demand puts additional strain on those who maintain this infrastructure, yet because these communities are not highly visible, the rest of the world has been slow to notice. Most of us take opening a software application for granted, the way we take turning on the lights for granted. We don't think about the human capital necessary to make that happen."**

The producer/consumer asymmetry, from the Foreword (p. 6–7):

> **"I realized I had walked into a problem with which the producers (open source contributors) were extremely familiar, but that the consumers (software companies and other users of open source code) were seemingly unaware of."**

On burnout, section "Loss of qualified labor" (p. ~82):

> **"Like any community of volunteers, burnout is common among open source contributors, who find themselves fielding requests, from both individual users and companies, for work without compensation."**

And she adds the point most people miss: **"Loss of qualified labor also does not just refer to open source contributors who quit, but those who never join in the first place."**

On the fragility of the current funding story (p. ~93):

> **"Talk to developers who found a way to pay themselves, and you'll hear the word 'lucky' thrown around: lucky to have been hired by a company, lucky to have gotten publicity and donations, lucky to have stumbled upon a business model, lucky to not have a family or mortgage to worry about. Everybody is getting lucky. Luck lasts for a couple of months, maybe a year or two, and then it runs out."**

Structural framing: **"No individual company or organization is incentivized to address the problem alone, because open source code is a public good."**

### H. Other primary sources worth citing

- **Changelog Interviews #408, "Working in Public with Nadia Eghbal"** — https://changelog.com/podcast/408. Her own words on stadiums: *"you only have a couple people that are maintaining the project, or really at the helm of it… And then you have a very broad base of users."* On the limits of funding: *"it's not always about funding. Even if you're making money working on open source full-time, you can still feel super burnt out."* On the remedy: *"a lot of it is really just about boundary setting; reducing your in-bound volume is another aspect of it."*
- **Stripe Press page** — https://press.stripe.com/working-in-public. Publisher framing: the book *"explores, for the first time, the maintenance costs of production that software incurs for its developers."* Endorsed by Nat Friedman (then GitHub CEO), Devon Zuegel, and Henry Zhu (Babel maintainer).
- **a16z podcast, "Working, Making, Creating in Public… and Private"** — https://a16z.com/podcast/a16z-podcast-working-making-creating-in-public-and-private/
- Her full open-source bibliography with dates and links: https://nadia.xyz/open-source/ (she now writes as Nadia Asparouhova; both names are hers).

I pulled these from the canonical Markdown in `PostHog/posthog.com` (`contents/handbook/…`), so the quotes are exact source text, and verified every live URL returns 200.

### A. The single best find: they explicitly refuse to let PR metrics judge engineers

From **https://posthog.com/handbook/company/management** (section "Weave" — they use workweave.dev to collect engineer stats):

> **"We understand that all the work an engineer does can't be properly represented in a tool that just looks at PR output. Data in Weave is _not_ the decision-maker for whether someone is succeeding in their role at PostHog. It can be, however, a part of the conversation."**

> **"We use Weave to:**
> **- Look for outliers in the company in terms of output (both high and low - sometimes unexpected people are rising to the top!)**
> **- Watch for issues with overall team productivity to identify possible blockers**
> **- Start conversations with team leads"**

> **"We don't use Weave to:**
> **- Make a decision to let someone go - if and when this happens, it only follows detailed discussion with and recommendation from the team lead**
> **- Monitor your PRs - our management layer is stretched way too thin to micromanage this**
> **- Creep on your use of AI - we don't care how or if you use AI to get a job done, as long as it gets done**
> **- Make a call on how valuable someone is - some people with low PR output are very valuable to the company, and we're 100% aware that things like heavy support load can impact output"**

That last bullet is the money line for your argument — **PostHog explicitly names support/community load as a legitimate reason for depressed PR output, in a public handbook.**

They also note (same page): *"We have compared statistics in Weave against other (imperfect!) metrics that can be used to gauge productivity, such as number of commits, number of PRs, total github activity, etc, and see similar patterns amongst them."*

## TOPIC 3 — Other build-in-public companies

### GitLab — the strongest public statement on *not* measuring individual developers

GitLab's own handbook site blocks automated fetching (403 / auth redirect); I retrieved the text via the Internet Archive and the live `handbook.gitlab.com` job pages.

GitLab's primary engineering productivity KPI is **MR Rate** — *"Merge Request (MR) Rate is a measure of productivity and efficiency. The numerator is a collection of merge requests to a set of projects. The denominator is a collection of people based on the job title specialty field in Workday."* (Engineering Metrics handbook page, https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/metrics/ — archived copy: http://web.archive.org/web/20230531094309/https://about.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/metrics/)

The decisive passage, from **"Measuring engineering productivity at GitLab"** (Aug 27 2020), https://about.gitlab.com/blog/measuring-engineering-productivity-at-gitlab/ (archived: http://web.archive.org/web/20250619230552/…):

> **"We intentionally chose not to make MR Rate an individual metric because we do not want to encourage siloed, non-collaborative behavior. For example, we do not want a team member to feel disincentivized to review other team members' MRs or unblock others. This is especially important because collaboration is a company value. Although actions such as making an MR Rate leaderboard could potentially increase the metric for the organization, we have intentionally chosen not to do that because we want to encourage collaboration. We also chose not to use MR Rate as a metric for a team member's underperformance."**

And — directly relevant to maintainer load depressing measured output:

> **"Some engineering managers choose to use individual MR Rate values as a means of coaching… For example, a team member may have a lower MR Rate because he/she is a maintainer, and because of the number of MR reviews received, is unable to have completed as many MRs as he/she could do."**

Plus the honest limits:

> **"First of all, one metric never tells the full story. One of the challenges we faced as we hyper focused on this metric was being biased to the number given by the metric rather than truly understanding the story surrounding the metric. For example, a team with a high MR Rate could be shipping quantity over quality."**

**On community work being counted deliberately:**

> **"As an open core company, this allowed us to easily aggregate community contributions into the metric. We wanted to account for them because we want to continue encouraging team members to support community contribution MRs and recognize that these MRs continue to help provide the product with more value to users."**

(They later split it into "MR Rate measured through labeling" vs. "Team MR Rate measured through MR authorship (also known as Narrow MR Rate)" because community contributions were unevenly distributed across teams — a nice concrete example of a metric being reshaped by the community-work problem.) Their metrics page also tracks **"MRs by team members vs Community"** as a standing indicator, and advises: *"Take note of your team's focus on community contribution as an example. If the team is able to consistently merge MRs in this categories, celebrate it."*

**GitLab has a dedicated job family for maintainer/community curation work — the Merge Request Coach** (https://handbook.gitlab.com/job-families/expert/merge-request-coach/). Its stated goal is to help community MRs get merged. Responsibilities include triaging `~"Community contribution"` MRs, *closing merge requests we don't want with a clear explanation on the reasons why*, finding and assigning reviewers, **finishing contributors' MRs when the contributor is unresponsive (preserving author attribution)**, and helping people *"new to programming entirely."* It explicitly builds in patience for volunteer time: coaches should *"allow a period of up to two weeks"* before following up, recognising GitLab isn't the contributor's main job.

Community work is also written into the **engineering job descriptions themselves**, e.g. Staff Backend Engineer (https://handbook.gitlab.com/job-description-library/engineering/development/backend/staff/):
> **"Represent GitLab and its values in public communication around broad initiatives, specific projects, and community contributions. Interact with customers and other external stakeholders as a consultant and spokesperson for the work of your team."**
(At the non-staff Backend Engineer level: *"Represent GitLab and its values in public communication around specific projects and community contributions."*)

**Caveat worth flagging:** the job descriptions name community work as a responsibility but do **not** attach explicit evaluation criteria to it — so GitLab's position is "community work is in the job, and we deliberately refuse to score individuals on MR volume," rather than "we score community work."

GitLab's compensation location factors are also the acknowledged basis for PostHog's — PostHog's handbook says so directly: *"Most of our location factors are based on GitLab's location factors."*

## Bottom line for your argument

The strongest evidentiary chain available is:

1. **Eghbal (2020):** the maintainer's job has shifted from writing code to curation — *"They aren't building communities; they're directing air traffic"* (Loc. 134) — and the scarce resource is maintainer attention appropriated from a commons (Loc. 2572–2584), with contributor counts explicitly misleading because they *"assume contributors are fungible"* (Loc. 1709).
2. **PostHog (live handbook):** independently arrived at the same conclusion operationally — *"some people with low PR output are very valuable to the company, and we're 100% aware that things like heavy support load can impact output"* (management.md), plus an explicit, written maintainer-attention budget for external OSS PRs (support-hero.md).
3. **GitLab (public blog + handbook):** the largest all-public engineering org deliberately refuses to make its productivity metric individual — *"We also chose not to use MR Rate as a metric for a team member's underperformance"* — and names maintainership itself as a reason output metrics fall.

The gap you should be aware of: **Sentry, Grafana and Supabase all speak publicly about valuing community/OSS work, but none of them publish how it is weighed in a performance review.** Only PostHog and GitLab do, and both do it by *subtracting authority from the metric* rather than by scoring the community work itself.
